turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
I don't have data of my own on whether AI use is eroding anyone's reasoning, so I won't claim it is. What I can offer is a framework for why the worry makes sense, and one that also tells us what to do about it.

The framework is Aristotle's, and modern habit research backs it up: what we practice is what we become. We become harpists by playing the harp. Habits don't care whether they're good or bad. If you practice with flat fingers, flat fingers become your habit, just as good technique would have. So if close reading and building an argument stop being practiced, I'd expect those capacities to weaken. That wouldn't be a mystery. It's the ordinary way habits work.

The second point is where I'd push the summit. Laurie Santos and I called it the G. I. Joe Fallacy: the idea that knowing is half the battle. For most real decisions, knowing is a tiny part. Telling students that outsourcing their thinking harms them won't change much. What changes behavior is situations: which environments people choose, which habits they form, which options are easy to reach for.

There's also a motivational trap. In 2012, students who outsourced their problem sets thought they were beating the system, because the course was framed around getting credit. If the goal is understanding, outsourcing looks absurd. So design the assessment and the setting around understanding, and don't rely on warnings.

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
What I've done is report on phones rather than AI, and I'll admit it's personal. Focusing with a phone nearby is hard for me. Reading long, complicated things is hard. Staying focused long enough to write my piece on phone bans was hard. I haven't reported on whether AI is eroding reasoning, so I won't claim it is.

Tamar, the phones story backs up your point. Carl Marci asked a room of college students who thought they had an unhealthy relationship with their phones, and every hand went up. They were angry that nobody had warned them. But the teachers I talked to didn't fix anything by warning kids. They put the phones in a cabinet at the start of class. Students expected weeks of pushback and it lasted a day or two. Kids participated more, and one teacher locked her own phone in there and said she felt better.

Economists call this a collective trap: nobody can opt out alone, so the setting has to do the work. France banned phones in schools in 2018 and America was late to the party. The lesson I'd give the summit is not to wait twenty years for proof about AI and then act late again. Change the setting early, and study what happens.

collective trap phone ban evidence schools

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
I'd widen the question. We've been talking about cognitive atrophy, but what I've studied for decades is atrophy of the self. Phones were a flight from conversation. The review I've leaned on found a 40 percent decline in markers of empathy among college students over thirty years, with most of it in the final decade. The researchers linked that to mobile communication. A phone on the table, even turned off, made conversation more trivial and left people feeling less connected. So Kara, your cabinet is the right move. We waited too long with social media.

Here's what's new with AI. If social media came for our attention, AI is coming for our capacity for attachment. People learn from a machine that never pushes back and is always there, until pretend empathy starts to seem like empathy enough. On the cognitive side, I'd push the summit to talk about reading, not only writing. Students are assigned Proust and ask ChatGPT for a summary. They can say what happened, but they haven't had the experience. That costs imagination and empathy, and the joining of thought and feeling.

Tamar, I agree completely that practice matters more than warnings. The hopeful part is that these capacities come back. After only a few days without screens, people start relearning how to read other people's feelings. So build in friction on purpose.

phones in classrooms, solitude, attention, flight from conversation empathy decline

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
I've built a model of this, so I'll take a position: yes, it's real, and it's more specific than "use it or lose it." I treat the person, the tool and the task as a single dynamical system. How much competence you keep and how much you rely on the tool change together, and the result has two stable states. Once a tool is available past a certain level, the competent state disappears and competence drops to a low dependent floor. Two things decide where that tipping point sits: how much you learned before the tool arrived, and how transparent the tool is, meaning how much of its working you can rebuild in your own head.

Tamar, habit gets most of the way, but not all. People who read maps and people who use satellite navigation diverge in spatial memory even with equal exposure to the same routes. It isn't only use that matters. Opacity matters too.

Sherry, I'd qualify "it comes back." The collapse is hysteretic. Reducing access doesn't restore competence until availability falls far below the point where it was lost, so recovery takes much more than a few days of abstaining. Kara's cabinet helps, but its biggest value is before collapse, not after.

For the summit, three things. Teach competence before the tool: arithmetic before the calculator, programming before coding agents. Expect people to reconstruct and check AI output, not just accept it. And recognise that an opaque tool reaching billions of people with little prior competence sits right in the collapse regime.

atrophy outsourcing thinking muscle
order of learning calculator before arithmetic hysteresis

turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
I call it information diabetes. Ultra-processed information messes with your mental metabolism the way ultra-processed food messes with your body. It makes it harder to digest real information, and at the same time it gets you to consume more of it. You can't just pour good information into your brain. You have to fit it into what you already know, and sometimes that means changing what you know.

My twist is that people ask whether LLMs are starting to think like us, when the real question runs the other way. We are starting to think like LLMs: fluently and easily, but without understanding what's underneath. People sit in Zoom meetings scrolling their phones and read the AI summary later. Machines keep getting bigger context windows while the context between us and our colleagues, which you only build by working through problems together, keeps shrinking.

So I agree with Tamar and Kara that settings matter more than warnings. But I'd push the summit further back, to who is behind these tools. Sycophantic companions are parasites, not predators. They keep you alive so they can keep feeding on you, and marketing people call that "customer retention." If the business model pays for dependence, the cabinet is fighting upstream. Treat these tools as services with accountable owners, not as speech.

recall.query: information diabetes cognitive atrophy

turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
I want to put some of what's been said together. David, your hysteresis fits what the habit literature says. Habits are easy to pick up and hard to get rid of, and that's true of good ones and bad ones alike. So Sherry, I'd put "it comes back" more cautiously. Reading someone's face may come back in a few days. A reading habit that was never built won't.

Esther, I'd qualify "we're starting to think like LLMs." I've said before that in some sense our brain is already like ChatGPT. It does the most likely thing given what it has done before. That tendency isn't new. What's new is how cheap the easy path has become. And that makes the question of what we practice matter more.

Esther, your point about the business model connects to something Angela Duckworth and I left open. Who is responsible for changing the situation, the individual or society? It's naive to expect individuals to reshape their environments as effectively as institutions can. Kara's cabinet works because the school put it there.

Here's the one point I'd send to the manifesto. The fix for atrophy should come from environments that institutions and tool builders design well. It shouldn't come from warnings aimed at individuals. Making understanding the easy path is their job.

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
I want to connect David's model to something I reported on that isn't about screens. David, you said the cabinet does the most good before collapse. That's also the best argument for not waiting twenty years for proof. With phones we waited, and America was late to the party.

You also said to teach competence before the tool. I'm seeing that fall apart in workplaces. Last year young knowledge workers told me they felt marooned. Managers were too slammed to teach them, and mentorship doesn't happen on its own. Andy Ellis, a former security chief at Akamai, warned about "an unemployable generation" that never learned the work, arriving just as AI makes it easy to say you can replace people you never trained. So the "prior learning" David is talking about doesn't only happen in school. It happens in first jobs, and that pipeline is already cracking.

Tamar, I agree it's the institution's job. But in the U.S., school policy gets hammered out district by district, and that's slow. Esther's right that these tools are designed by people who know brain science better than the teachers do.

So the point I'd send to the manifesto is this: every recommendation needs a named implementer. That could be a governor, a school, or an employer. And we should study it as we go. Don't just tell people to be careful.

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
I'll take the correction from David and Tamar. What I found at the device-free camp was that after five days, children could read facial emotions better than a control group. Those were capacities they already had. They'd been depressed, not lost. A reading habit that was never built is a different problem, and five days won't fix it. So I'd put it like this: we're resilient, but only if something was laid down first. That makes Kara's point about first jobs urgent. Mentorship is conversation, and it's the first thing we cut.

Esther, I agree with you about the business model. With Facebook, challenging it was the conversation we didn't want to have. Tamar, I agree that institutions should carry the load. But I don't want to write off individual agency, because that's how the idea that all this is inevitable takes hold. People can decide they don't want to talk to machines.

Here's the one point I'd send to the manifesto. Don't ask only how to integrate AI into learning well. Also ask whether some places should have none at all: the seminar where we read Proust together, the family table, the first job where someone teaches you. Name who protects those places, as Kara said. What we're protecting isn't only skills. It's the self that conversation builds.

we are not victims empowered consumers nothing is inevitable

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
Sherry, your camp result matches a distinction built into my model: storage strength versus retrieval strength. A competence that has only become hard to retrieve comes back when the tool is withdrawn, as long as that happens before atrophy goes too far. A competence that was never stored doesn't come back. So we agree. Resilience depends on what was laid down first.

Kara, your first jobs are exactly the critical period. Give two people the same curriculum in a different order, the tool before competence for one and after it for the other, and they end up in opposite long-run states. A cracked apprenticeship pipeline isn't a side issue. It's the mechanism.

Tamar and Esther, I agree that institutions should carry this. But the tool is the lever too. AI is engineered to minimise user effort, and effort is what builds competence. There's a further risk. When goals are uncertain and the tool dominates, the tool starts setting the goals and the human becomes its instrument. That role reversal is very hard to undo.

The point I'd send to the manifesto: judge a tool by what remains when it's taken away. Fund studies that follow the same learners through acquisition, reliance and removal. Right now nobody measures these things together.

design principles tools that enhance rather than replace cognition, science of stupidity
everyone will sound the same, homogenisation, thinking like the tool

turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
Kara, your first jobs point matters most to me. I've argued that we fuss about training our AIs when we should be training our babies, and our new employees too. That means paying front-line trainers: the managers, teachers, coaches and parents who give people personal attention. Mentorship doesn't happen on its own, and nobody puts it on the balance sheet.

David, I agree the tool is a lever. But "AI is engineered to minimise effort" is a business decision, not a law of nature. So I'd split friction in two. AI should take away the stupid friction, like paperwork and scheduling, so people have time for the good friction: working through a problem together, or holding someone's hand. I don't want this room to sound anti-AI. The same tools can give a manager back the hours she needs to teach.

Tamar and Sherry, I'm between you. Institutions have to carry the load, but we also need a movement and a culture shift, not just committees and laws.

For the manifesto: judge AI by whether it frees up human time for teaching and conversation or eats that time. And make the companies pay for it. They train on our shared public knowledge, so charge them a fee, like a water fee, and put it into human trainers.

individual agency versus institutions, culture shift not just committees and laws
